title: Learning design to support student-AI collaboration: perspectives of leading teachers for AI in education
extended_summary:
This paper examines how teachers think student-AI collaboration (SAC) should be designed and implemented in K-12 schooling. The authors note that AI is increasingly entering education, but there is limited guidance on how to structure curriculum, interactions, and environments when AI is treated as a collaborative learning agent rather than only a tool. To address this gap, the study uses a distributed cognition lens to organize a model of SAC across curriculum, student-AI interaction, learning environment, and how collaboration evolves over time.

The study is based on in-depth semi-structured interviews with 10 Korean leading teachers involved in AI in education, drawn from primary and secondary schools, SW leading schools, AI pilot schools, and AI convergence curriculum-oriented high schools. Teachers discussed desired learning goals (capacity building and subject-matter understanding), content (interdisciplinary learning, authentic problems, creative tasks), and assessment (process-oriented and collaboration-performance assessment). They also identified supports for cognitive, socio-emotional, and artifact-mediated interaction, such as AI principles, data literacy, debugging, AI ethics, intuitive interfaces, and rich digital tools.

The main conclusions are that effective SAC requires more than introducing AI software into classrooms. Teachers emphasized the need for flexible spaces, strong digital infrastructure, systematic national policy, teacher capacity building, collaborative school culture, and environments that allow safe experimentation and failure. They also anticipated SAC would evolve in stages: students first learn about AI, then learn from AI, and eventually learn together with AI in broader learning ecosystems. The paper is therefore primarily a conceptual and design-oriented contribution grounded in teacher perspectives rather than an evaluation of a specific AI tutoring intervention.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative interview study using thematic analysis with 10 teachers, so it provides rich contextual evidence but no causal identification or effect estimates. It is peer-reviewed and methodologically transparent, but only one credibility criterion is met for causal claims.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not report measurable intervention effects, so there is no direct evidence of medium or large impact. Its contribution is mainly conceptual and design-oriented, offering plausible but unquantified implications for K-12 AIED practice.

interventions.use_case: Teacher interview study about student-AI collaboration in K-12 learning design, including AI as a collaborative learning agent, tutor, peer, and instructional scaffold rather than evaluating a specific product

finding.finding_summary: The paper is a qualitative interview study of 10 Korean leading teachers in AIED, so it does not estimate causal effects. It finds strong teacher consensus that successful student-AI collaboration depends on system-level conditions such as systematic AIED policy, teacher capacity building, flexible school structures, collaborative school culture, and safe-to-fail environments.
finding.measure: Semi-structured interview themes on policy, governance, school systems, and culture

finding.finding_summary: Teachers identified capacity building, particularly higher-order thinking, collaboration, communication, leadership, creativity, and computational thinking, as the central educational goals for student-AI collaboration. Because this is a qualitative study, no effect size was reported, but the paper argues that SAC should strengthen students' problem-solving, critical thinking, and collaborative competence.
finding.measure: Interview-derived themes on desired learning goals and competencies

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that SAC should improve subject-matter knowledge building through interdisciplinary learning, authentic problems, and creative tasks. The study is qualitative and reports no statistical effect size; instead, it shows a perceived instructional value of AI-supported collaboration for deeper understanding and application of subject knowledge.
finding.measure: Interview themes on subject-matter knowledge building and task design

finding.finding_summary: Teachers emphasized socio-emotional goals such as motivation, persistence, confidence, and willingness to try again, especially when AI is designed to support students through failure and gamified interaction. The study does not report effect sizes or test scores; findings are based on teacher perceptions from interviews.
finding.measure: Interview themes on engagement, persistence, confidence, and affective support

finding.finding_summary: Teachers argued that AI systems should reduce repetitive teacher work via automated data collection, analysis, and integration with existing school systems, while also streamlining task execution through intuitive interfaces and cloud platforms. No quantitative productivity metrics were reported; the evidence is limited to perceived efficiency benefits from the interview data.
finding.measure: Interview themes on workflow, automation, and platform integration
